newsitem.title: USA: EPA proposes pollution standards for trains.
newsitem.headline: EPA proposes pollution standards for trains.

text.p: The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency Friday proposed its first-ever standards for air pollution from diesel locomotives, which it said would cost the industry $76 million a year.

The new standards to curb emissions of nitrogen dioxide, a component of smog, would be phased in beginning on January 1, 2000, with further reductions of nitrogen dioxide and cuts in soot emissions in 2005.
The standards would apply to new train engines and older engines as they are remanufactured.
A typical locomotive can produce as much nitrogen oxide a in one year as 3,000 cars, according to the agency.
When fully in effect, the standards should slash nitrogen oxide emissions by two-thirds or 600,000 tons annually and cut emissions of particulate matter or soot in half or by 10,000 tons, EPA said.

Unlike cars, locomotives are often in service for 40 or more years and remanufactured several times in their life span. "The long service life makes fleet turnover occur less frequently than any other category of mobile sources," EPA said.
The railroad industry considered the proposed standards fair, although they were more stringent than the industry had envisioned in a voluntary plan.

"A national approach is the only way to avoid a patchwork of state requirements that would make our railroads less, rather than more, efficient," said Richard Russack, vice president of corporate relations for Burlington Northern Santa Fe Corp.
"Further reductions are technically supportable and would probably avoid environmental harm that would occur if less freight were shipped by rail," Russack said.

"EPA struck a good balance between the nation's environmental needs and the potentially crippling economic impact of overly stringent locomotive standards," Russack said on behalf of the Association of American Railroads.
EPA's $76 million a year estimate for the cost of complying with the standards might turn out to be low if locomotives end up having to use more fuel per mile with the new engines.
"Because those engines haven't been built or used yet, you don't know if you're going to have a fuel benefit or a fuel loss," Russack said.
